claim_decisions.statement: In 13 Basse-Casamance communities, 234 agricultural interviewees reported environmental and rainfall change alongside widespread food-access difficulties; these are selected respondents' experiences, not national prevalence or climate attribution.
claim_decisions.uncertainty: Purposive, cross-sectional interviews; study field dates are unspecified. The published food-insecurity percentages have an unclear item denominator and are not reproduced.

SEN-SRC-101.methodology: Public-good experiment with332 analyzed participants after five exclusions from337;14focus groups. Coordinator read the publisher DOI redirect.
SEN-SRC-101.limitations: Artificial collective-risk treatment and game cooperation are not observed climate impacts or violence; study municipalities are unnamed.

pathways.climate_pressure: Participants in selected Basse-Casamance communities described irregular rainfall and environmental degradation.
pathways.documented_impact: The same participatory study reports food-access difficulties and disrupted agricultural livelihoods.
pathways.fcv_mediator: Landmines, fear and displacement restrict access to farmland and production, narrowing livelihood options under environmental stress.
pathways.possible_consequence: These constraints can leave climate-sensitive food systems less able to absorb further shocks; the interaction is conditional, not a measured joint causal effect.
alternative_explanations: Poverty, markets, salinization, deforestation and labor constraints can affect food access independently of conflict-climate interaction.
pathways.uncertainty: One purposive cross-sectional study combines respondent perceptions with historical context. It does not estimate a climate-conflict interaction, current mine prevalence or a national effect.
resilience_factors: Participants propose reforestation, sustainable farming and stronger environmental governance; their effects were not evaluated.
pathways.compact_statement: In selected Casamance communities, mines and displacement restrict farming under environmental stress; a conditional reverse-FCV vulnerability mechanism, not climate-caused violence.

executive_assessment.text: Studies in the Groundnut Basin, Ferlo/Louga and Casamance add local livelihood and institutional detail. An experiment documents group-biased cooperation under simulated risk; it is not evidence that a climate event caused violence.

Casamance interviews describe conflict-related restrictions on land and food production under environmental stress. The assembled reverse-FCV mechanism is explicitly conditional and not a national causal estimate.

The R4 evaluation reports reach and resilience-related gains but also transfer, monitoring and inclusion weaknesses. The accessible publisher summary cannot establish effect sizes or independent attribution.
